findings.title: Production Processes & Technology
findings.claim: The Nissan plant in Sunderland produces a car every 67 seconds
findings.finding: Wrong by nearly 2x. All official Nissan sources and independent media consistently state Nissan Sunderland produces one car every two minutes (~120 seconds). The 67-second figure does not appear in any verifiable source. The 11-million-milestone Nissan press release (June 2023) explicitly uses 'a car every two minutes for 37 years'.

findings.title: Motivation
findings.claim: John Lewis famously pays an annual 'Partnership bonus' to every partner when the business is in profit.
findings.finding: Factually inaccurate as a general rule. JLP has refused to pay the bonus in 2021, 2023 and 2024, explicitly citing investment priorities even after returning to profit. In March 2024, despite reporting a £56m profit, JLP announced no bonus for the third time in four years. The bonus is discretionary, not guaranteed when profitable. The claim teaches students that profit automatically triggers the bonus, which is incorrect.
findings.recommended_fix: Change to: 'John Lewis has historically paid an annual Partnership bonus to every partner — a share of profits — though this is at the discretion of management and has not been paid in some years despite the business returning to profit.'

findings.title: Analysing Financial Performance
findings.claim: Luxury brands like Burberry run 15-20% net margins.
findings.finding: Severely out of date and currently misleading. Burberry's reported net profit margin for FY2023/24 was approximately 0% (the company posted an operating loss in H1 2024/25 and a £41m reported loss in November 2024). While Burberry did achieve ~15-16% net margins in 2019-2021, it is now in a well-publicised financial crisis. Using Burberry as a current example of high luxury margins gives students a factually wrong picture. The 15-20% range may hold for the strongest luxury houses (Hermes, LVMH) but not Burberry specifically in 2024-25.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace 'Luxury brands like Burberry run 15-20%' with a more accurate example (e.g. Hermes ~25%, or note that Burberry's margins declined sharply in 2023-24). If Burberry must be named, add a note that its margins have fallen significantly in recent years.

findings.title: Motivation
findings.claim: A retail assistant on £11.44 an hour (the 2024–25 UK minimum wage for those 21+)
findings.finding: The £11.44 rate applied from April 2024 to March 2025 only. From April 2025 the National Living Wage (NLW) for those aged 21+ rose to £12.21. Labelling £11.44 as the '2024-25' rate is now out of date; any student reading in 2025-26 will find the actual rate is £12.21. The rate also changed name/eligibility in April 2024 (previously NLW was 23+; it was extended to 21+ from April 2024). The lesson appears to have been written accurately for 2024 but has not been updated.
findings.recommended_fix: Update to: '£12.21 an hour (the 2025-26 National Living Wage for those aged 21+)'. Remove year from inline text or use a generic reference to 'current NLW' with a note to verify the latest rate at gov.uk.

findings.title: Production Processes & Technology
findings.claim: Warburtons bakes thousands of white loaves, cleans down the ovens and changing lines, then bakes the same quantity of wholemeal [as a batch production example].
findings.finding: Oversimplification. Warburtons primarily uses the Chorleywood Breadmaking Process, a high-speed semi-continuous system producing over 2 million items/day at up to 160 units per minute per line — more characteristic of flow production than classic batch. While different bread types are produced and lines are switched, the clean-down-and-reset narrative implies a smaller-scale batch operation. This risks students applying the wrong classification to a real company. Warburtons itself is more accurately described as flow (for standard loaves) with batch elements for specialist products.
findings.recommended_fix: Use a cleaner batch-production example (e.g. a regional artisan bakery, or a pharmaceutical manufacturer) or add a nuance note that large bread manufacturers blend flow and batch methods.

findings.title: Production Processes & Technology
findings.claim: Amazon's fulfilment centres use more than 750,000 mobile robots
findings.finding: The 750,000 figure was accurate as of mid-2023 when Amazon announced it had reached that milestone. As of early 2025 Amazon has stated it has deployed over 1 million robots. The figure is no longer current but is not actively misleading for GCSE purposes — the point (scale of automation) stands.
findings.recommended_fix: Update to 'over one million robots' to reflect the current figure.

findings.title: Production Processes
findings.claim: The Nissan Sunderland plant produced its ten-millionth car in 2019
findings.finding: Confirmed accurate. The 10-millionth vehicle was built on 20 June 2019 — a Vivid Blue Nissan Qashqai Tekna. Multiple official Nissan sources and news outlets confirm this date.

findings.title: Production Processes
findings.claim: Lean production was developed by Toyota in Japan
findings.finding: Confirmed accurate. The Toyota Production System (TPS), developed by Taiichi Ohno and Eiji Toyoda between 1948 and 1975, is the direct precursor to what MIT researchers later named 'lean production' in their 1990 publication 'The Machine That Changed the World'. The lesson's attribution is correct.

findings.title: Production Processes
findings.finding: Confirmed accurate. Toyota Manufacturing UK (TMUK) has its vehicle assembly plant at Burnaston in Derbyshire and hosts the Toyota Lean Management Centre there.

findings.title: Production Processes
findings.claim: Pret A Manger: anything unsold by the end of the day is given to charity rather than warehoused
findings.finding: Confirmed accurate. The Pret Foundation has since 1995 collected unsold food at end of day and distributed it to charity partners (FareShare, The Felix Project, City Harvest). Pret donates approximately 1.7 million food items annually to the homeless. The claim in the lesson accurately represents this policy.

findings.title: Analysing Financial Performance
findings.claim: Supermarkets typically run net margins of 2-5%
findings.finding: Broadly accurate. Tesco's net margin is approximately 3-4% and Sainsbury's similar. The CMA 2024 report and Unite analysis confirm combined Big 3 profit margins around 4.3% in 2021/22. The 2-5% range is a fair GCSE-level approximation.
